Every manuscript from the eleven Qumran caves and the other Judaean Desert sites. Search or filter the list, open a manuscript's full surviving text with English beside it, or jump to its photographs.

"Read" opens the manuscript in its original language (Hebrew, Aramaic or Greek) with English beside it. Restored letters are in grey, and the reader explains the other marks. "Photos" opens the manuscript in the Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library, which has high-resolution and infrared images of the fragments.

"Frags" counts a long scroll's columns or a broken one's fragments, and "Lines" counts lines with surviving text. Both come from the Abegg–Bowley–Cook transcriptions, so they're blank where that dataset has no text, such as for the Greek papyri.

The biblical English is the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, which is public domain, shown verse by verse. Where a scroll's wording differs from the standard Bible, the English won't show it.

The rest was translated line by line for this catalogue using AI and spot-checked against the Hebrew. It's a reading aid: before quoting it, check a published translation such as Vermes, or Wise, Abegg and Cook. Fragments too broken to make sense of are shown in the original only.

No open transcription exists for the Greek biblical scrolls from Qumran and Nahal Hever, so for those "Read" shows the Septuagint text of the verses each fragment comes from, clearly labelled. The letters and documents of the Bar Kokhba revolt and the Babatha archive are listed one by one, each with its Greek, Hebrew or Aramaic text.

How to read a siglum like 4QpaleoDeutʳ

A siglum gives the cave number, the site (Q = Qumran), the script or material, the work, and a letter for which copy it is. So 4QpaleoDeutʳ is the 18th copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, written in Paleo-Hebrew script. Each manuscript also has a plain number, such as 4Q45. More in the guide.

p pesher, a commentary (1QpHab)
pap written on papyrus, not parchment
ar in Aramaic
gr in Greek
tg targum, an Aramaic translation
apocr apocryphon, a retold or extra-biblical work
S Serekh, the Community Rule
D the Damascus Document
M Milhamah, the War Scroll
H Hodayot, the Thanksgiving Hymns
T the Temple Scroll
MMT Miqsat Ma'ase ha-Torah
Mur Wadi Murabba'at
Hev Nahal Hever
Mas Masada
PAM a fragment known only by its Palestine Archaeological Museum photo number

Sources

  • List of manuscripts: the Wikipedia list of the Dead Sea Scrolls (CC BY-SA), merged with the scroll inventory of the ETCBC Dead Sea Scrolls dataset. Titles follow the standard DJD catalogue (E. Tov, Revised Lists of the Texts from the Judaean Desert, 2010).
  • Hebrew and Aramaic text: transcriptions by Martin Abegg, James Bowley and Edward Cook, via the ETCBC (CC BY-NC 4.0).
  • Greek documents from Nahal Hever and Wadi Murabba'at: the Duke Databank of Documentary Papyri, via papyri.info (CC BY 3.0). Hebrew and Aramaic Bar Kokhba letters: the Hebrew Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). Septuagint context for the Greek scrolls: H. B. Swete, The Old Testament in Greek (public domain), digitised by Eliran Wong.
  • Biblical English: The Holy Scriptures According to the Masoretic Text (Jewish Publication Society, 1917; public domain), via the Sefaria export archive.
  • Other English: a new AI translation made for this catalogue. A sample was independently checked against the Hebrew, and every line was then scanned for dropped negations and other common slips.
  • Photographs: Leon Levy Dead Sea Scrolls Digital Library, Israel Antiquities Authority.

Dates and identifications of small fragments are often uncertain and debated; check the Leon Levy library or the DJD volumes before citing a detail.
